name: Jordan's nose in the locker room

parameters.label: Minutes in the room
parameters.explain: With a steady smell, the sense of smell becomes much less sensitive within about 10 minutes.

parameters.label: Window or fan
parameters.explain: Tests the 'the smell went away' idea: airing the room really does lower the smell in the air. Was the room aired?

parameters.label: Break outside first
parameters.explain: After 10 minutes in the room he steps out. Away from the smell, his nose and brain reset — so coming back, it hits him again.

parameters.label: How strong the smell is
parameters.explain: How many sweaty kits and shoes are in the room after a hot practice.

parameters.label: Stuffy nose
parameters.explain: A nose stuffed up by a cold keeps smell molecules from reaching the smell-sensing cells.

rules.N: Sst * 10 * pow(0.5, m * W / 5) * (1 - 0.35 * st) * (floor + (1 - floor) * (1 - min(b, 1) * (1 - pow(0.5, 10 / adapt)) * pow(0.5, b / reset)) * pow(0.5, m / adapt))

overlay.caption: smell stays in the air · smell sensors and brain quiet down · the alarm stops

explain.summary: Smell-sensing cells in Jordan's nose send messages to his brain when smell molecules reach them. A new smell sets off a strong alarm. But when the smell stays the same, the system quiets down — within minutes he barely notices it, even though the smell is still in the air. Step outside for a few minutes and it resets, so walking back in, the smell hits him again.
rules: The smell in the air stays the same unless the room is aired.
How strongly he notices it drops by half about every 3 minutes, down to a small leftover.
Away from the smell, his sense of smell resets, halving the 'used to it' effect about every 2 minutes.
A stuffy nose cuts how much smell reaches the sensors.

source.fact: Smell-sensing cells in the nose connect directly to the brain and send it messages when they detect odour molecules; a nose stuffed up by a cold keeps odours from reaching them.
In a study of 80 people breathing a steady rose-like smell, their smell thresholds were already clearly raised (they had become less sensitive) after 10 minutes, and more so after 2 hours.
The brain gets used to a constant smell and ignores it until there is a big enough change to get its attention.

choice.what: Noticing halves every 3 minutes, down to 15% of the start
choice.why: Chosen to match Jordan's clue (strong at the door, almost gone after 10 minutes) and the study's 'clearly less sensitive after 10 minutes'.

choice.what: After stepping out, the 'used to it' effect halves every 2 minutes
choice.why: Recovery away from a smell is quick; we don't have a measured number for teens, so this is a teaching value.

choice.what: Receptors and brain are counted together
choice.why: Both the smell-sensing cells and the brain adapt; separating them would add detail without changing the lesson.

choice.what: An open window halves the smell every 5 minutes; a fan doubles that
choice.why: A simple way to show airing really removes smell from the air.

illustrative: Jordan is fictional; the smell strength and the percentages are made-up scales.
The 70% at the door and 16% after 10 minutes match the story, not a measurement.
provenance.studying: Scientists are still working out how much of 'nose blindness' happens in the nose itself and how much in the brain.

citations.supports: Our brains get tired of registering the same things and ignore a constant smell until there's a big enough change to get their attention; the brain constantly adapts to everything we sense.

does: Shows the smell staying in the air while noticing it fades
Shows a short break resetting the nose
Lets you test whether airing the room could explain it
doesnt: Measure any real person — Jordan is fictional and the numbers are illustrative
Tell different smells apart, or model smells that are harmful to breathe
Separate adaptation in the nose from adaptation in the brain
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: If you smell gas or smoke, don't wait to 'get used to it' — get out and tell an adult right away.
